title: Cerebral palsy, Autism and Cystic Fibrosis

los.text: Recognise abnormal motor development and link to diagnosis and intervention.
sessions: Abnormal motor development in a child
los.html:
Typical gross motor milestoneMedian ageRed flag (limit age)
Good head control3 monthsPoor head control at 4 months
Sits unsupported6–8 monthsNot sitting by 9 months
Crawls / bottom-shuffles, pulls to stand9 months
Walks independently12 monthsNot walking by 18 months (check CK in boys: Duchenne)
Runs, climbs stairs2 years
Hops4 years
Signs of abnormal motor development
  • Hand preference before 12 months (suggests hemiplegia)
  • Persistent primitive reflexes after ~6 months (Moro, asymmetric tonic neck)
  • Abnormal tone (floppy or stiff)
  • Asymmetry of movement
  • Persistent toe walking
  • Abnormal posture
  • Loss of skills (regression).
CausesCerebral palsy, neuromuscular disease (SMA, Duchenne), global developmental delay, genetic syndromes, spinal dysraphism, hypothyroidism, neglect.
Diagnosis
  • History (antenatal, birth, neonatal, family)
  • Examination (tone, power, reflexes, posture, primitive reflexes, spine, skin)
  • Early CP detection in high-risk infants with the General Movements Assessment and HINE before 5 months' corrected age
  • MRI brain
  • CK
  • Genetics
  • TFTs
  • Metabolic tests.
InterventionEarly referral to the child development team: physiotherapy, OT, SALT, orthoses, family support; early therapy uses brain plasticity.

los.text: Know the variations in the presentation of cerebral palsy and link them to neurological signs.
los.html:
Cerebral palsy
  • a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance in the developing fetal or infant brain (up to ~2 years)
  • ~2 per 1000 births
  • Motor features may change as the child grows even though the lesion doesn't.
Causes
  • Antenatal (most: infection, stroke, malformations), perinatal (hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy), postnatal (meningitis, head injury including NAI, kernicterus, hypoglycaemia)
  • Prematurity is the biggest risk factor (periventricular leukomalacia).
DistributionTypical presentationUsual cause
Hemiplegia (one side, arm > leg)Early hand preference, fisting, tiptoe on one sidePerinatal stroke
Diplegia (legs > arms)Toe walking, scissoring gait, tight hamstrings and adductorsPrematurity (PVL damages fibres to the legs near the ventricles)
Quadriplegia (all four limbs + trunk)Severe motor impairment, often epilepsy, learning disability, feeding problems, scoliosisSevere HIE, extensive injury
Neurological signsSpastic (UMN): velocity-dependent increased tone, brisk reflexes, clonus, upgoing plantars; dyskinetic: dystonia, chorea, athetosis; ataxic: hypotonia, poor balance, intention tremor.
Associated problems
  • Epilepsy
  • Learning disability
  • Visual and hearing impairment
  • Speech and swallowing difficulties (aspiration, faltering growth)
  • Drooling
  • Reflux
  • Constipation
  • Hip displacement (hip surveillance X-rays)
  • Scoliosis
  • Contractures
  • Pain
  • Sleep and behaviour problems.
Management (MDT)
  • Physio, OT, SALT, dietitian
  • Orthoses (AFOs)
  • Spasticity: baclofen, botulinum toxin, intrathecal baclofen, selective dorsal rhizotomy
  • Orthopaedic surgery (tendon lengthening, hip surgery)
  • Dystonia: trihexyphenidyl
  • Drooling: glycopyrronium
  • Gastrostomy
  • Epilepsy treatment
  • Education support
  • GMFCS levels I–V describe function.

los.text: Know the prevalence of Autism Spectrum Disorders and link it to their aetiology, diagnostic features, assessment and variations in presentation.
los.html:
PrevalenceAbout 1–2% of children; diagnosed 3–4 times more often in boys (girls are under-diagnosed, partly through masking).
Aetiology
  • Highly heritable (~80%; polygenic plus de novo variants)
  • Linked with fragile X, tuberous sclerosis, Down syndrome, prematurity, prenatal valproate, older parental age.
  • Not caused by vaccines (the MMR claim was fraudulent).
Diagnostic features (both needed, from early childhood, causing impairment)
Social communication and interaction: limited social-emotional reciprocity (sharing interests, back-and-forth conversation), non-verbal communication (eye contact, gestures, facial expression), difficulty developing and maintaining relationships
  • Restricted, repetitive behaviours and interests: stereotyped movements (hand flapping, rocking)
  • Echolalia
  • Insistence on sameness and routines
  • Intense narrow interests
  • Sensory over- or under-reactivity (noise, textures, food)
Assessment (NICE CG128)
  • Refer to the autism assessment team (paediatrician, psychologist/psychiatrist, SALT)
  • Developmental history, structured observation (ADOS-2), parental interview (ADI-R), school/nursery information
  • Examination (skin for tuberous sclerosis, dysmorphism, head circumference)
  • Hearing test
  • Genetic tests (microarray, fragile X) if indicated.
Coexisting conditionsADHD, learning disability, epilepsy, anxiety, sleep problems, constipation, selective eating, developmental coordination disorder.
Variation
  • a wide spectrum of support needs, language and intellectual ability
  • Girls may show subtler social difficulties, masking and more socially typical interests
  • Many people are diagnosed as adults.

los.text: Know the differential diagnosis of musculoskeletal causes of limp
los.html:
AgeMusculoskeletal causes of limp
Any ageTrauma (fractures, soft tissue), septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, non-accidental injury, malignancy (leukaemia, bone tumours), JIA, reactive arthritis
1–3 yearsToddler's fracture (spiral tibial fracture), DDH (late presentation), septic arthritis, NAI
3–10 yearsTransient synovitis (commonest cause; after a viral illness), Perthes disease (4–8), JIA
10–16 yearsSUFE (often obese boys; may present with knee pain), Osgood–Schlatter, osteochondritis dissecans, sports injuries, stress fractures, bone tumours (osteosarcoma, Ewing's)
FootSever's disease (calcaneal apophysitis), foreign body, ingrown toenail, poorly fitting shoes

los.text: Know the common neurological conditions that cause limp, explain the significance of referred pain
los.html:
Neurological causeClues
Cerebral palsy (hemiplegia, diplegia)Toe walking, spasticity, brisk reflexes
Duchenne muscular dystrophyBoys, Gowers' sign, waddling gait, calf pseudohypertrophy, very high CK
Spinal muscular atrophyWeakness, absent reflexes, fasciculations
Peripheral neuropathy (Charcot–Marie–Tooth)Pes cavus, foot drop, high-stepping gait
Spinal cord lesions (tethered cord, spinal dysraphism, tumour)Sacral dimple or hair tuft, bladder/bowel problems, asymmetric leg signs
Posterior fossa tumour, acute cerebellar ataxia (post-varicella)Ataxic gait, headache, vomiting
Guillain–Barré syndrome, transverse myelitisAcute weakness, areflexia
  • Referred pain: hip pathology often presents as knee pain (shared supply from the obturator and femoral nerves): always examine the hip in a child with knee pain (SUFE, Perthes).
    • Others: discitis (refuses to walk or sit, back pain)
    • appendicitis or psoas abscess (flexed hip)
    • testicular torsion (groin and thigh pain)
    • abdominal or pelvic masses.

los.text: Know why a child may limp with reference to their age
los.html:
AgeWhy these causes
Toddlers (1–3)
  • Learning to walk → falls → toddler's fracture
  • Can't describe or localise pain (just refuse to bear weight)
  • Septic arthritis more likely (in infants, metaphyseal vessels cross the growth plate, so osteomyelitis spreads into joints)
  • NAI risk
  • Late-presenting DDH shows once walking
Young children (3–10)
  • Transient synovitis after viral infections common at this age
  • Perthes: the femoral head epiphysis has a precarious blood supply in this window (avascular necrosis, mostly boys 4–8)
  • JIA
Adolescents (10–16)
  • Growth spurt: the physis is weak relative to growing body weight and hormonal changes → SUFE (especially obese, or with hypothyroidism)
  • Apophyses under traction from strong muscles → Osgood–Schlatter, Sever's
  • Sport → overuse and stress injuries
  • Bone tumours peak with rapid bone growth (osteosarcoma)
Any ageInfection, malignancy (leukaemia peaks at 2–5), inflammatory arthritis

los.text: Know the investigations required to differentiate causes of limp in children
los.html:
InvestigationHelps with
FBC (with film)Infection (WCC), leukaemia (cytopenias, blasts)
CRP, ESRInfection, inflammation (Kocher criteria)
Blood culturesSeptic arthritis, osteomyelitis
CKMuscular dystrophy
ANA, RFJIA (ANA positive → uveitis screening)
LDH, uric acid, filmMalignancy
X-ray (affected area; AP pelvis + frog-leg lateral for hips)Fractures, Perthes, SUFE, tumours, osteomyelitis (late)
Skeletal surveySuspected NAI
Ultrasound hipEffusion (transient synovitis vs septic); guides aspiration
Joint aspirationGram stain, culture, cell count: urgent if septic arthritis possible
MRIOsteomyelitis, early Perthes, occult fractures, tumours, discitis
Kocher criteria(septic arthritis of the hip)Non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5 °C, ESR >40, WCC >12 × 10⁹/L (more criteria = higher probability).
Red flagsFever, systemically unwell, night pain, weight loss or sweats, non-weight-bearing, age under 3, inconsistent history or bruising (NAI).
Examine everythingGait, all joints, spine, abdomen, testes, neurology, skin (purpura, bruising).

los.text: Know the causes of limp associated with joint or bony problems in a child
los.html:
ConditionFeaturesManagement
Septic arthritisHot, swollen joint, won't move it, fever, unwell; S. aureus (Kingella kingae in under 4s)Emergency: aspirate, IV antibiotics, surgical washout
OsteomyelitisBone pain and tenderness (metaphysis), feverMRI, cultures, IV antibiotics
Transient synovitis3–8 years, after a viral illness, well, afebrile or low fever, partial weight-bearing; a diagnosis of exclusionRest, NSAIDs, safety-net; resolves in 1–2 weeks
Perthes disease
  • Boys 4–8
  • Insidious limp, hip or knee pain, ↓ abduction and internal rotation
  • X-ray: flattening, fragmentation, sclerosis of the femoral head
Observation, physio, bracing or osteotomy; younger = better prognosis
SUFE
  • 10–15, obese, boys
  • Hip, thigh or knee pain, externally rotated leg, obligatory external rotation on hip flexion
  • Frog-leg lateral X-ray (Klein's line)
  • Bilateral in up to a third
Urgent surgical pinning; non-weight-bearing
DDH
  • Risk: breech, family history, female, first-born
  • Barlow/Ortolani at newborn check
  • Ultrasound by 6 weeks if risk factors
  • Late: limp, leg length difference, asymmetric skin folds, limited abduction
Pavlik harness (<6 months), surgery later
JIA
  • Arthritis >6 weeks in a child <16
  • Oligoarticular (commonest, young girls, ANA+ → uveitis screening), polyarticular, systemic (fever, salmon-pink rash, hepatosplenomegaly), enthesitis-related, psoriatic
NSAIDs, intra-articular steroids, methotrexate, biologics
Osgood–SchlatterAdolescent athletes, tender tibial tuberosityRest, ice, activity modification
FracturesToddler's, Salter–Harris (growth plate), stressImmobilise; consider NAI
Bone tumoursOsteosarcoma (adolescents, metaphysis around the knee, sunburst, Codman's triangle), Ewing's (diaphysis, "onion skin"), osteoid osteoma (night pain relieved by NSAIDs)Urgent referral
LeukaemiaBone pain, limp, pallor, bruising, infectionsUrgent FBC and film

los.text: Understand the concept of learning disability.
los.html:
• Learning (intellectual) disability: a significantly reduced ability to understand new or complex information and learn new skills (impaired intelligence, IQ <70), with a reduced ability to cope independently (impaired adaptive/social functioning), starting before adulthood with a lasting effect.
SeverityIQ (approximate)
Mild (most common)50–69
Moderate35–49
Severe20–34
Profound<20
Not the same as a specific learning difficulty (dyslexia, dyspraxia), which doesn't affect general intellect.
Causes
  • Genetic (Down syndrome: commonest genetic cause; fragile X: commonest inherited cause; Rett, Angelman, Prader–Willi, Williams, tuberous sclerosis, PKU)
  • Prenatal (fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis, valproate, hypothyroidism)
  • Perinatal (extreme prematurity, HIE)
  • Postnatal (meningitis, encephalitis, head injury including NAI)
  • Often unknown.
Health inequalitiesPeople with learning disabilities die decades earlier on average (LeDeR reviews), often from avoidable causes (aspiration pneumonia, epilepsy, constipation, sepsis, late cancer diagnosis), partly from diagnostic overshadowing.
Responses
  • Annual health checks from age 14 (GP register)
  • Reasonable adjustments (Equality Act 2010)
  • Hospital passports
  • Learning disability liaison nurses
  • Mandatory Oliver McGowan training
  • and never assuming lack of capacity (MCA).

los.text: Identify the major developmental milestones and important red flags for abnormal development in a child.
los.html:
AgeGross motorFine motor and visionSpeech and hearingSocial
6 weeksLifts head briefly proneFixes and followsStartles to noiseSocial smile
3 monthsGood head controlHands together, holds a rattleCoos, turns to soundLaughs
6 monthsSits with support, rollsReaches, palmar grasp, transfers objectsBabblesMouths objects
9 monthsSits unsupported, crawls, pulls to standInferior pincer grip"Mama/dada" (non-specific), understands "no"Stranger anxiety, peek-a-boo
12 monthsCruises, first stepsFine pincer grip, points1–3 words with meaningWaves bye-bye, plays pat-a-cake
18 monthsWalks well, squatsTower of 3, scribbles, spoon6–20 words, points to body partsSymbolic play, copies household tasks
2 yearsRuns, kicks a ballTower of 6, draws a line2-word phrasesParallel play
3 yearsJumps, pedals a tricycleTower of 9, copies a circle3–4-word sentencesPlays with others, shares
4 yearsHops, stairs like an adultCopies a cross and squareTells stories, asks "why?"Cooperative play, dresses
Red flags (refer)
Loss of skills at any age (urgent)
  • No social smile by ~8 weeks
  • Not fixing and following by 3 months
  • Concerns about vision or hearing at any age (absent red reflex, squint, nystagmus: urgent)
Not sitting unsupported by 9 months; not walking by 18 months
Hand preference before 12 months
No pointing or shared attention by 12–18 months; no words by 18 months; no two-word phrases by 2½ years
Abnormal tone, persistent toe walking, head circumference crossing centiles, parental concern
  • Use corrected age for babies born preterm until 2 years.

los.text: Know the various clinical presentations of cystic fibrosis and how to diagnose cystic fibrosis.
los.html:
• Cystic fibrosis: autosomal recessive, CFTR gene (chromosome 7)
    • commonest variant F508del
    • about 1 in 2500 UK births
    • 1 in 25 white Europeans are carriers.
Presentation
Newborn blood spot screening (day 5): raised immunoreactive trypsinogen → CFTR variant testing → sweat test
Meconium ileus (10–20% of neonates), prolonged jaundice
Faltering growth, steatorrhoea (pale, greasy, offensive stools), rectal prolapse
Recurrent chest infections, chronic productive cough, bronchiectasis, clubbing
Nasal polyps, sinusitis
Male infertility (congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens)
Salty-tasting skin, hyponatraemic dehydration in heat, pancreatitis, diabetes, liver disease
  • Diagnosis: sweat test (pilocarpine iontophoresis): chloride ≥60 mmol/L = CF (30–59 intermediate; <30 unlikely), plus two disease-causing CFTR variants
    • faecal elastase (low = pancreatic insufficiency)
    • CXR, sputum culture, lung function.

los.text: Know the multiorgan damage caused in cystic fibrosis.
los.html:
• Mechanism: CFTR is a cAMP-regulated chloride channel
    • when faulty, epithelia secrete too little Cl⁻ (and absorb more Na⁺ via ENaC), so secretions are dehydrated, thick and sticky.
OrganDamage
Lungs
  • Low airway surface liquid
  • → poor mucociliary clearance
  • → chronic infection and neutrophilic inflammation
  • → bronchiectasis
  • → respiratory failure (main cause of death).
  • Organisms: S. aureus (early), H. influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (chronic, mucoid), Burkholderia cepacia complex (transmissible, poor prognosis), non-tuberculous mycobacteria, Aspergillus (ABPA)
  • Haemoptysis, pneumothorax
Upper airwaySinusitis, nasal polyps
Pancreas
  • Blocked ducts → exocrine insufficiency (~85%): malabsorption, steatorrhoea, fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency, faltering growth
  • CF-related diabetes (common in adults)
  • Pancreatitis
GutMeconium ileus, distal intestinal obstruction syndrome, rectal prolapse, reflux, constipation
LiverFocal biliary cirrhosis → portal hypertension; gallstones
Reproductive
  • Men: congenital absence of the vas deferens → obstructive azoospermia (sperm can be retrieved for ICSI)
  • Women: thick cervical mucus, reduced fertility
Sweat glandsCan't reabsorb Cl⁻ → high sweat chloride, salt loss, hyponatraemic dehydration
Bones and jointsOsteoporosis, arthropathy
OtherKidney stones, drug toxicity (aminoglycosides), psychosocial burden

los.text: Link pharmacological and other treatments to underlying physiology and pathology in cystic fibrosis.
sessions: Current and future treatments in cystic fibrosis
los.html:
TreatmentPhysiological target
  • CFTR modulators: correctors (elexacaftor, tezacaftor, lumacaftor) help misfolded CFTR reach the membrane
  • Potentiators (ivacaftor) increase channel opening
  • Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor for anyone with ≥1 F508del (from age 2)
Fix the faulty protein: large improvements in lung function, sweat chloride, weight and exacerbations; monitor LFTs; CYP3A4 interactions
Airway clearance physiotherapy (daily: active cycle of breathing, PEP devices, exercise)Mechanically clear thick mucus
Dornase alfa (rhDNase)Cleaves neutrophil DNA in sputum → thinner mucus
Hypertonic saline (nebulised), inhaled mannitolRehydrate airway surface liquid
Prophylactic flucloxacillin (young children, UK)Prevent S. aureus infection
Pseudomonas eradication (oral ciprofloxacin + nebulised colistin) on first isolation; nebulised antibiotics for chronic infection (colistin, tobramycin, aztreonam); long-term azithromycinReduce bacterial load and inflammation
Exacerbations: 14 days of two IV anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (e.g. ceftazidime + tobramycin)Treat infection
Infection control (segregation of CF patients)Prevent cross-infection (Pseudomonas, Burkholderia)
Pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon) with all meals and snacksReplace lipase etc.: fat absorption
High-calorie, high-fat diet, vitamins A, D, E, K, salt supplementsMake up malabsorption and salt loss
Insulin (CF-related diabetes), ursodeoxycholic acid (liver), bisphosphonates (bones), laxatives (DIOS), steroids + itraconazole (ABPA)Manage organ complications
Lung transplantationEnd-stage lung disease
  • Outlook: median predicted survival is now over 50 years and rising with modulators
    • MDT CF centre care, psychological support, fertility support (ICSI), transition to adult services.

los.text: Interact with clinicians and families of ex-premature children
los.html:
• Common issues for ex-premature children (risk rises with lower gestation, especially <28 weeks):
AreaProblems
NeurodevelopmentCerebral palsy, cognitive and learning difficulties, ADHD, autism, coordination problems
SensesRetinopathy of prematurity (visual impairment), hearing loss
LungsBronchopulmonary dysplasia (home oxygen, wheeze), severe RSV (palivizumab/nirsevimab for high risk)
Growth and feedingFaltering growth, oral aversion, tube feeding
GutEffects of necrotising enterocolitis (stomas, short bowel), hernias
FamilyParental anxiety, depression or PTSD after NICU, financial and work strain
Practice
  • Use corrected age for growth and development until 2 (vaccines at chronological age)
  • Developmental follow-up (NICE NG72: enhanced support for the highest-risk babies, with assessments around 2 years corrected age and later).
Talking with families and clinicians
  • Acknowledge the NICU journey
  • Listen to parents' expertise
  • Be honest about uncertainty
  • Family-centred care
  • Coordinate the MDT (neonatal outreach, community paediatrics, physio, OT, SALT, health visitors, education)
  • Signpost (e.g. Bliss).

los.text: Describe the barriers (e.g., communication, physical access, social stigma) that individuals with intellectual disabilities face when accessing healthcare services.
sessions: Learning Disability team – Paul Ridd and Your Voice Advocacy
los.html:
BarrierExamples
CommunicationDifficulty describing symptoms or pain; clinicians not adapting language; information not in easy-read
Diagnostic overshadowingSymptoms or behaviour change attributed to the learning disability, so illness is missed
Physical accessWheelchair access, couches, scales, waiting areas
Sensory and environmentalNoise, bright lights, crowds, long waits (especially with autism)
SystemPhone-based booking, short appointments, letters they can't read, fragmented services, low screening uptake
Dependence on othersNeed carers for transport and attendance
Consent and capacityAssumptions that the person lacks capacity, or carers deciding for them
Attitudes and stigmaLack of training and confidence among staff; inappropriate DNACPR decisions
FearNeedles, procedures, previous bad experiences
  • Consequences: worse health and premature, avoidable deaths.

los.text: Demonstrate effective communication techniques tailored to the needs of individuals with intellectual disabilities, using clear language, visual aids, or alternative methods
sessions: Learning Disability team – Paul Ridd and Your Voice Advocacy
los.html:
Technique
Prepare: read the hospital/health passport, ask carers how the person communicates, offer a longer appointment at a quiet time
Speak to the person directly, not only to the carer
Short, simple sentences, one idea at a time, concrete words, no jargon or metaphors
Allow extra time; be patient; repeat
Visual aids: pictures, easy-read leaflets, symbols, Makaton/signing, objects, demonstration on a model ("show, then do")
Check understanding: ask them to show or tell you
Watch for non-verbal cues of pain or distress (DisDAT)
Offer choices; respect preferences
Involve carers and family (with consent) and the learning disability liaison nurse
Make reasonable adjustments (desensitisation for blood tests, sedation plans, home visits)

los.text: Identify the key signs and symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in children based on clinical observations and history
los.html:
DomainSigns in children (NICE CG128)
Social communication
  • Reduced or absent response to name
  • Reduced eye contact
  • Reduced social smiling
  • Limited joint attention (doesn't point to show or follow your point by 12–18 months)
  • Few gestures (waving)
  • Little imitation or pretend play
  • Prefers to play alone
LanguageDelayed or unusual: echolalia, pronoun reversal, monotone, scripted or very literal language; difficulty with conversation
Restricted and repetitiveHand flapping, rocking, spinning, lining up toys, intense unusual interests, insistence on sameness, distress at change
SensoryOver- or under-reaction to noise, textures, light, pain; selective eating; sensory seeking
RegressionLoss of words or social skills (often 15–24 months): needs urgent assessment
  • History: developmental history, pregnancy and birth, family history, behaviour across settings (nursery/school reports), regression; observe the child.

los.text: List and explain common differential diagnoses for ASD in children, considering developmental, neurological, and psychological conditions
los.html:
DifferentialDistinguishing points
Hearing impairmentDoesn't respond to sounds: test hearing in every child
Developmental language disorderLanguage delay but good social interest and non-verbal communication
Global developmental delay / intellectual disabilityDelay across all areas, social skills in line with developmental age
ADHDInattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity (often coexists)
Selective mutism, anxietySpeaks normally at home
Attachment disordersHistory of neglect or institutional care
Rett syndromeGirls, regression, hand-wringing, slowing head growth (MECP2)
Landau–Kleffner syndromeLoss of language with epileptic EEG
Fragile X, tuberous sclerosisGenetic syndromes (often coexist with autism)
Visual impairmentReduced eye contact
OthersFASD, OCD, tic disorders, very early-onset psychosis (rare), abuse, normal variation (shyness)

los.text: Identify post-diagnostic support services available for children with ASD, including therapeutic, educational, and familial resources
los.html:
SupportExamples
Information and family supportExplain the diagnosis, written report, key worker; parent programmes (e.g. EarlyBird, Cygnet)
Communication and developmentSocial communication interventions with parents and teachers, SALT, OT (sensory and motor)
EducationAdditional learning needs support: in Wales an Individual Development Plan (ALN Act 2018), in England an EHCP; specialist provision
HealthTreat coexisting conditions: ADHD, anxiety (CAMHS), sleep (sleep hygiene, melatonin), epilepsy, constipation, selective eating (dietitian)
Behaviours that challengePositive behaviour support; antipsychotics only for severe behaviour alongside psychosocial approaches
Social care and financesShort breaks/respite, carers' assessments, benefits (DLA, Carer's Allowance)
CommunityNational Autistic Society, Integrated Autism Service (Wales), peer support groups; transition planning
  • Avoid unproven treatments (chelation, secretin, exclusion diets); no medication treats the core features.

los.text: Define and classify the different types of cerebral palsy (CP), including spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, and mixed types, based on clinical features
los.html:
TypeLesion siteFeaturesProportion
SpasticPyramidal (motor cortex, white matter: PVL, stroke)Velocity-dependent ↑ tone, brisk reflexes, clonus, upgoing plantars, contractures; hemiplegic, diplegic or quadriplegic~80%
DyskineticBasal ganglia / thalamus (acute profound HIE, kernicterus)Dystonia, chorea, athetosis; fluctuating tone; involuntary movements worse with emotion or effort~5–10%
AtaxicCerebellumHypotonia, poor balance, broad-based gait, intention tremor, dysmetria~5%
MixedSeveral areasOften spastic + dyskinetic
DistributionUnilateral (hemiplegia) or bilateral (diplegia, quadriplegia).
FunctionGMFCS level I (walks without limitation) to V (wheelchair-transported, very limited head and trunk control).

los.text: Recognise the key clinical features of cerebral palsy (e.g., motor impairment, spasticity) and list common differential diagnoses (e.g., static encephalopathy, genetic syndromes, metabolic disorders)
los.html:
Key clinical features of CP
Delayed motor milestones
Abnormal tone: often early hypotonia, then spasticity or dystonia
Persistent primitive reflexes (Moro, ATNR) beyond ~6 months
Early hand preference, asymmetry, fisting
Toe walking, scissoring, abnormal posture
Feeding and swallowing problems
Associated: epilepsy, learning disability, visual/hearing impairment, speech problems
  • Red flags that it may not be CP: progression or regression
    • family history
    • consanguinity
    • normal MRI
    • fluctuating or paroxysmal symptoms
    • abnormal eye movements
    • isolated hypotonia with weakness.
DifferentialClue
Genetic syndromes (hereditary spastic paraplegia, Rett)Progressive spastic diplegia; regression in girls
Metabolic disorders (glutaric aciduria type 1, mitochondrial disease, leukodystrophies, lysosomal storage disease, Lesch–Nyhan)Regression, episodes of decompensation, self-injury (Lesch–Nyhan)
Dopa-responsive dystoniaDiurnal variation; dramatic response to levodopa (always consider a trial)
Neuromuscular (Duchenne, SMA, congenital myopathies)LMN signs, weakness, reduced reflexes, high CK
Spinal cord lesions (tethered cord, tumour, dysraphism)Back signs, bladder/bowel problems, normal upper limbs
Brain tumour, hydrocephalusProgression, raised ICP, large head
Ataxia-telangiectasia, Friedreich's ataxiaProgressive ataxia; telangiectasia, infections
Static encephalopathy from other causes, NAIHistory
  • Investigations: MRI brain (abnormal in most: PVL, infarct, malformation)
    • metabolic and genetic tests if atypical
    • CK
    • EEG if seizures
    • hip X-rays
    • vision and hearing tests.

los.text: Identify histopathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease, Lewy bodies and vascular dementia.
los.html:
ConditionGross brainHistological hallmarksStains
Alzheimer's diseaseDiffuse cortical atrophy, worst in the medial temporal lobes (hippocampus) and parietal lobes; wide sulci, enlarged ventricles (hydrocephalus ex vacuo)Extracellular β-amyloid (neuritic/senile) plaques; intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau); neuronal loss; cerebral amyloid angiopathy; granulovacuolar degeneration, Hirano bodiesSilver stains, Congo red (amyloid: apple-green birefringence), tau and Aβ immunohistochemistry
Lewy body disease (dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson's)Pale substantia nigra and locus coeruleus; cortex relatively spared or mild atrophyLewy bodies: round eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions of α-synuclein with a pale halo (brainstem: classical; cortex: less distinct); Lewy neuritesα-synuclein and ubiquitin immunohistochemistry
Vascular dementiaMultiple infarcts (large-vessel territories or many small lacunes in the basal ganglia, thalamus, white matter); white matter pallorArteriolosclerosis (hyaline thickening of small vessels), small infarcts with gliosis and macrophages, white matter rarefaction (demyelination, loss of axons), microbleedsH&E, myelin stains (Luxol fast blue)
  • Clinical links: Alzheimer's: early memory loss (hippocampus)
    • Lewy body: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, neuroleptic sensitivity
    • vascular: stepwise decline, focal signs, vascular risk factors.
  • Mixed pathology (Alzheimer's + vascular) is common in older people.
